body_markdown:
***Is your property technology working as hard as your team? Or is it quietly creating more problems than it solves?***


In multifamily, technology is supposed to make operations easier. It should save time, streamline processes, improve the resident experience, and give property teams better information to make smarter decisions.


But what happens when your technology isn't doing any of those things? It might be time for a PropTech checkup.


Think of your technology ecosystem like a patient in the emergency room. Some systems may be perfectly healthy; others might need a little attention, and a few could be costing your organization time, money, and productivity without anyone realizing just how sick they are.


##


**PropTech Diagnosis**


###


**Symptom [#1](https://www.bgsf.com/blogs/hashtags/1) : Your Team Has Developed a Lot of Workarounds**


***Diagnosis: Technology isn't supporting the workflow.***


When employees start creating spreadsheets, side processes, sticky notes, or manual workarounds to compensate for a technology platform, pay attention.


A workaround here and there isn't necessarily a crisis. But when workarounds become part of the daily routine, there is probably a larger underlying issue.


Ask your team:


-


What technology-related tasks take longer than they should?


-


Where are you entering the same information more than once?


-


What do you track outside of your primary systems?


-


What processes still require manual intervention?


-


Which platforms do you avoid using unless absolutely necessary?


Your team shouldn't have to become technology engineers just to get their jobs done.


###


**Symptom [#2](https://www.bgsf.com/blogs/hashtags/2) : Your Technology Isn't Talking to Your Other Technology**


**Diagnosis: Integration complications.**


Your property management system, CRM, accounting software, and other PropTech solutions may all serve important purposes. But if they don't communicate effectively, your team can end up spending valuable time moving information from one system to another.


That creates more than an inconvenience. Manual data entry can introduce errors, create duplicate work, and make it harder to know which information is actually accurate.


A healthy technology ecosystem should make information easier to access, not create another obstacle between your team and the information they need.


###


**Symptom [#3](https://www.bgsf.com/blogs/hashtags/3) : You're Paying for Features Nobody Uses**


**Diagnosis: Technology bloat.**


More technology doesn't automatically mean better technology. It's easy to accumulate platforms over time when a new tool solves one problem, another gets added for a different department, then someone finds a solution with a promising AI feature.


Before long, your organization has a technology stack that looks impressive on paper but isn't necessarily delivering value.


Take a closer look at what you're actually using. Are employees using the features you're paying for? Are multiple platforms performing similar functions? Are there tools that seemed valuable during implementation but have since become underused?


Sometimes the healthiest technology decision isn't adding another platform. It's figuring out whether you need the ones you already have.


###


**Symptom [#4](https://www.bgsf.com/blogs/hashtags/4) : Your Team Doesn't Know What the Data Is Telling Them**


**Diagnosis: Information overload.**


Technology should help property teams make decisions. But more dashboards, reports, and data points don't necessarily lead to better decisions. If every department has its own reports, metrics, or versions of the truth, your technology ecosystem may be producing information without producing clarity.


A healthier approach starts with a few basic questions:


-


What do we actually need to know?


-


Who needs to know it?


-


How frequently do they need it?


-


Where does that information come from?


-


Can we trust it?


The goal is not to collect more data. It's to make the right data accessible, understandable, and actionable.


###


**Symptom [#5](https://www.bgsf.com/blogs/hashtags/5) : Employees Aren't Using the Technology Correctly**


**Diagnosis: Training deficiency—or a usability problem.**


If your team isn't using a platform as intended, it's tempting to blame adoption. But before scheduling another training session, ask whether the technology itself is part of the problem.


Is the system intuitive? Does it fit naturally into existing workflows? Is the training relevant to employees' actual responsibilities? Do team members understand why the technology matters?


Training matters, but training can only go so far when the technology doesn’t align with the way people actually work.


It’s also worth looking at whether the training itself is relevant. Employees don’t necessarily need to know every feature a platform offers. They need to know how to use the features that matter to their roles. A property manager, leasing professional, maintenance team member, and regional leader may all interact with the same technology differently. Training should reflect those differences rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach.


###


**Symptom [#6](https://www.bgsf.com/blogs/hashtags/6) : Your Technology Decisions Are Being Made in a Vacuum**


**Diagnosis: Strategic disconnect.**


One of the biggest PropTech problems may have nothing to do with the technology itself. If technology decisions are being made without considering your organization's broader operational goals, you can end up with disconnected solutions that don't address the problems your teams actually face.


Before investing in another platform, consider the bigger picture.


-


What are you trying to improve?


-


Where are your biggest operational bottlenecks?


-


What does your team spend too much time doing?


-


Where are residents experiencing friction?


-


What information is difficult to access?


-


What processes could be automated?


Technology should be part of your operational strategy—not a collection of unrelated tools.


##


**So, What's the Treatment Plan?**


A complete technology overhaul may create more disruption than it solves, so it's best to start with a technology health check.


###


1. Take the patient's history.


Document the technology you're currently using. What does each platform do? Who uses it? How often? What does it cost? What other systems does it connect with?


###


2. Identify the symptoms.


Talk to the people actually using the technology every day. Find out where they're losing time, encountering frustrations, or creating workarounds.


###


3. Check for interactions.


Look at how your systems communicate—or don't communicate—with one another. Identify duplicate data entry, disconnected workflows, and opportunities for better integration.


###


4. Measure the vital signs.


Define what success looks like. Without measurable outcomes, it's difficult to know whether a technology investment is actually making your operation healthier.


###


5. Prescribe strategically.


Once you understand the problems, determine what needs to change. That could mean optimizing an existing platform, improving training, integrating systems, eliminating redundant tools, or implementing a new solution.


##


**Don't Wait for a PropTech Code Blue**


Technology problems rarely appear overnight. They usually start with small symptoms: an extra spreadsheet, a manual process, a report that takes hours to create, a feature nobody understands, or an employee who says, "That's just how we've always done it."


Individually, these issues may not seem urgent, but collectively, they can become a significant drain on your property team's time and productivity. That's why regular PropTech assessments matter. Instead of waiting until your technology ecosystem is in crisis, make technology health part of your ongoing operational strategy.
